name: Nineteen Eighty-Four
kicker: Orwell’s totalitarian nightmare · Gave English the word “Orwellian”
briefing: George Orwell imagined a future where the government, led by the shadowy Big Brother, controls not just what people do but what they’re allowed to think. Winston Smith secretly rebels against the all-seeing Party by falling in love and keeping a secret diary, in a world of telescreens, Newspeak, and doublethink. _Nineteen Eighty-Four_ has haunted readers — and politics — ever since it was published in 1949.

qb.tip: Mr Charrington’s shop and Room 101 are the two most reliable stock clues; Big Brother himself shows up in almost every giveaway line.

sample.note: the 5 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist is finally broken in Room 101 when his interrogator straps a wire cage full of hungry rats toward his face, the one thing he fears most in the world. He saves himself only by screaming for the torment to be turned on someone he loves instead.
tossups.r: That interrogator, O’Brien, had posed as a member of a secret resistance movement. For 10 points, name this dystopian novel about Winston Smith’s rebellion against a totalitarian party, written by George Orwell.

tossups.p: Citizens in this novel are watched at all times through two-way telescreens that can never be fully turned off, even at home. Suspicious behavior like an unusual facial expression, called facecrime, can draw the attention of the regime’s secret police.
tossups.r: That secret police, the Thought Police, arrests anyone suspected of disloyal thoughtcrime. For 10 points, name this novel about constant government surveillance in the superstate of Oceania.

tossups.p: This novel’s totalitarian party is slowly replacing Standard English with a stripped-down official language designed to make rebellious thoughts almost impossible to express. A character helping compile that language’s dictionary is abruptly erased from existence, becoming an “unperson.”
tossups.r: That language, Newspeak, aims to shrink the range of human thought by shrinking vocabulary itself. For 10 points, name this novel that also coined the term “doublethink.”

tossups.p: This novel’s characters practice holding two contradictory beliefs at once and sincerely accepting both, a mental skill its ruling party calls doublethink. Party slogans built on this same contradiction declare that “War Is Peace” and “Freedom Is Slavery.”
tossups.r: The party’s third slogan, “Ignorance Is Strength,” completes the trio. For 10 points, name this novel in which the Party controls thought itself through doublethink and Newspeak.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist works in the Records Department of the Ministry of Truth, rewriting old newspaper articles so that history always matches the Party’s current claims. Outdated documents are dropped down a chute called a memory hole to be incinerated.
tossups.r: Yet he secretly rebels by keeping a forbidden diary. For 10 points, name this novel about Winston Smith’s work erasing inconvenient facts for a totalitarian government.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist buys an old coral-and-glass paperweight from a junk shop run by a man named Mr Charrington. He later rents a room above that same shop to secretly meet a woman he has fallen in love with.
tossups.r: That shop turns out to be a trap run by the Thought Police all along. For 10 points, name this novel in which a hidden telescreen eventually exposes Winston and Julia’s affair.

tossups.p: This novel’s heroine openly wears the sash of the Junior Anti-Sex League while secretly breaking nearly every rule the Party sets for personal behavior. She first slips the protagonist a note reading “I love you” after stumbling in a hallway at work.
tossups.r: She and the protagonist, Winston, begin a secret affair that the Party treats as a political crime. For 10 points, name this novel in which Julia and Winston are eventually betrayed and arrested.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist trusts an Inner Party member who claims to belong to a resistance group called the Brotherhood, supposedly led by the shadowy traitor Emmanuel Goldstein. That member lends him a banned book about the Party’s true strategy.
tossups.r: The member, O’Brien, turns out to be a loyal agent who has been watching the protagonist for years. For 10 points, name this novel in which Winston is entrapped by the Party loyalist O’Brien.

tossups.p: This novel’s world is permanently divided among three warring superstates: Oceania, Eurasia, and Eastasia. During an annual Hate Week rally, the identity of Oceania’s enemy abruptly switches mid-speech, and the crowd instantly accepts the Party’s new version of history.
tossups.r: No one in the crowd dares question this sudden, obvious contradiction. For 10 points, name this novel set in Airstrip One, a province of the superstate Oceania.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist lives in Victory Mansions, next door to a fanatically loyal Party man named Parsons. Parsons is eventually denounced to the Thought Police and arrested after his own young daughter overhears him talking in his sleep.
tossups.r: That daughter belongs to the Spies, a youth group trained to inform on its own parents. For 10 points, name this novel about a surveillance state where even families can’t be trusted.

tossups.p: The lowest class in this novel, the proles, are left largely unwatched by the Party and allowed beer, pulp films, and a weekly National Lottery as a kind of pressure valve. This novel’s protagonist sometimes wonders whether real rebellion could only ever come from that class.
tossups.r: He studies the proles hopefully but never finds the resistance movement he’s looking for. For 10 points, name this novel about Winston Smith’s doomed search for freedom in a totalitarian state.

tossups.p: Strapped into a device that causes him pain whenever he answers incorrectly, this novel’s protagonist is slowly made to agree that two plus two can equal five, if the Party says so. His interrogator insists that the Party’s control of reality itself is absolute.
tossups.r: That interrogator, O’Brien, later sends him to Room 101 to finish breaking his spirit completely. For 10 points, name this novel about the limits of objective truth under a totalitarian party.

tossups.p: This novel opens, “It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.” A minor character named Syme, who works on a dictionary of the Party’s official language, later disappears from work without warning.
tossups.r: Syme has simply become an “unperson,” erased from every record as though he never existed. For 10 points, name this novel, which ends with its broken protagonist finally deciding that he loves Big Brother.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist repeatedly dreams of a peaceful, sunlit landscape he calls the Golden Country, which turns out to match a real field where he later meets his lover in secret. He also has fragmented memories of his mother and sister vanishing when he was a boy.
tossups.r: Those hazy childhood memories predate the Party’s full takeover of his country. For 10 points, name this novel narrated from inside the mind of Winston Smith.

tossups.p: This novel’s government runs four ironically named Ministries: the Ministry of Truth handles propaganda, the Ministry of Peace handles war, the Ministry of Plenty handles rationing and scarcity, and the Ministry of Love handles torture and interrogation.
tossups.r: Each Ministry’s real function is the exact opposite of its cheerful name. For 10 points, name this novel set in a totalitarian superstate ruled by Big Brother and the Party.

clues.t: Dystopian novel by George Orwell about a totalitarian superstate called Oceania
Protagonist Winston Smith works at the Ministry of Truth, rewriting history to fit the Party’s lies
The Party is led by the all-seeing, possibly fictional figurehead Big Brother
Citizens are watched through two-way telescreens and the Thought Police
Party slogans include “War Is Peace” and “Freedom Is Slavery”
Winston is tortured in Room 101 of the Ministry of Love, where prisoners face their own worst fear
Winston’s lover Julia secretly meets him above Mr Charrington’s antique shop
O’Brien pretends to belong to a resistance group called the Brotherhood, supposedly led by Emmanuel Goldstein
Winston is finally broken by his worst fear — rats — and betrays Julia to save himself
In his secret diary, Winston writes the forbidden words “DOWN WITH BIG BROTHER” over and over
The Party’s constructed language, Newspeak, is designed to make rebellious thoughts impossible to even express
Doublethink lets Party members sincerely hold two contradictory beliefs at once
Winston works in the Records Department, dropping inconvenient documents down a “memory hole”
Interrogated until he agrees that “two plus two makes five” if the Party says so
Goldstein’s banned book, _The Theory and Practice of Oligarchical Collectivism_, explains the Party’s real strategy
Oceania is one of three endlessly warring superstates, alongside Eurasia and Eastasia
During Hate Week, the enemy nation switches mid-speech and the crowd instantly accepts the new version of history
Julia openly wears the sash of the Junior Anti-Sex League while secretly breaking its rules
Neighbor Parsons is denounced to the Thought Police by his own fanatical child
Buys an old coral-and-glass paperweight from Mr Charrington’s shop
A coworker named Syme, who helps compile the Newspeak dictionary, is abruptly “vaporized” into an unperson
The novel opens, “It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen”
Ends with its broken protagonist finally deciding that he loves Big Brother

trap.title: The novel, or its dictator?
trap.body: “Big Brother” is the Party’s all-seeing figurehead inside the story — not the title of the book. Kids (and plenty of adults) mix them up constantly. Winston Smith is the hero, not the title either, and George Orwell is the author, who also wrote a very different dystopia, Animal Farm.
trap.fix: If the question asks you to “name this novel” or “name this work,” the answer is Nineteen Eighty-Four (or 1984), not Big Brother, Winston Smith, or George Orwell — and not Animal Farm, which is a totally different book by the same author.
